text.text: When electrons are scattered independently by impurities and by lattice vibrations, their scattering rates add and so do the resistivities, ρ(T)=ρimp+ρph(T),\rho(T)=\rho_{\rm imp}+\rho_{\rm ph}(T),ρ(T)=ρimp​+ρph​(T), where the residual resistivity ρimp\rho_{\rm imp}ρimp​ is independent of temperature and proportional to the impurity concentration, and ρph(T)\rho_{\rm ph}(T)ρph​(T) is a property of the pure host. Two samples of the same metal then have parallel ρ(T)\rho(T)ρ(T) curves, with a TTT-independent difference. In the Bloch–Grüneisen form ρph∝T5\rho_{\rm ph}\propto T^5ρph​∝T5 at T≪ΘDT\ll\Theta_DT≪ΘD​ and ∝T\propto T∝T at T≳ΘDT\gtrsim\Theta_DT≳ΘD​.Holds when Independent scattering mechanisms acting on the same carriers on one isotropic Fermi surface. Deviations of a few percent are routine in real metals (anisotropic scattering, multiband conduction, Kondo and size effects), and the rule is only a first approximation at high impurity concentrations.

In the relaxation-time approximation (em-6.4) ρ=m/ne2τ\rho=m/ne^2\tauρ=m/ne2τ and independent collision channels give 1/τ=1/τimp+1/τph(T)1/\tau=1/\tau_{\rm imp}+1/\tau_{\rm ph}(T)1/τ=1/τimp​+1/τph​(T). Impurity scattering is elastic and temperature-independent, phonon scattering freezes out as T→0T\to0T→0 (few phonons, and only small-angle scattering), producing T5T^5T5, while at high TTT the number of phonons is ∝T\propto T∝T. The rule can fail when the scattering rate is not the same for all carriers: with two groups of carriers in parallel the conductivities add and the resistivities do not.Within the stated constant-relaxation-time model, take independent exponential collision waiting times (constant hazards) with positive rates λimp\lambda_{\rm imp}λimp​ and λph\lambda_{\rm ph}λph​. Their no-collision indicators at time t≥0t\ge0t≥0 are bounded independent variables. Factoring the expectation of their product (prob 2.1.13) makes the probability of no collision in either channel the product e−λimpte−λpht=e−(λimp+λph)te^{-\lambda_{\rm imp}t}e^{-\lambda_{\rm ph}t}=e^{-(\lambda_{\rm imp}+\lambda_{\rm ph})t}e−λimp​te−λph​t=e−(λimp​+λph​)t. The mean waiting time is therefore 1/(λimp+λph)1/(\lambda_{\rm imp}+\lambda_{\rm ph})1/(λimp​+λph​). With the same carriers, density and mass in Drude's law, this gives the additive resistivities; it does not justify adding resistivities of separate parallel carrier populations. A zero-rate channel can be omitted; if both rates vanish, this model has no finite collision time.

Switch to two parallel bands (impurities scatter mostly the second band) and the curves are no longer parallel: the difference drifts with TTT, which is the failure of the rule. The readout gives the residual resistance ratio ρ(300 K)/ρ(4 K)\rho(300\,\mathrm K)/\rho(4\,\mathrm K)ρ(300K)/ρ(4K) of each sample.

text.text: A three-dimensional crystal with ppp atoms per primitive cell has exactly 3p3p3p phonon branches ωs(k)\omega_s(\mathbf k)ωs​(k), s=1,…,3ps=1,\dots,3ps=1,…,3p. Assume harmonic stability and no zero-frequency modes at k=0\mathbf k=0k=0 beyond the three rigid translations. Because the crystal is invariant under uniform translation, three of them are acoustic (ω→0\omega\to0ω→0 as k→0\mathbf k\to0k→0) and the remaining 3(p−1)3(p-1)3(p−1) are optical (ω(0)>0\omega(0)>0ω(0)>0). A crystal of NNN cells therefore has 3pN3pN3pN normal modes, one for each degree of freedom, and in the zone each branch has exactly NNN allowed wave vectors.Holds when Harmonic, stable crystals. The value ppp is the number of atoms in the primitive cell; counts of the individual symmetry types of branch (transverse/longitudinal) require the crystal's point group.

For each wave vector the equations of motion form a 3p×3p3p\times3p3p×3p Hermitian dynamical matrix D(k)D(\mathbf k)D(k), so it has 3p3p3p real eigenvalues ω2\omega^2ω2 (nonnegative for a harmonically stable crystal). At k=0\mathbf k=0k=0 a rigid translation of all atoms along xxx, yyy or zzz stretches no bond and so is a zero-frequency eigenvector: this is the acoustic sum rule, equivalent to ∑jΦij=0\sum_{j}\Phi_{ij}=0∑j​Φij​=0 and responsible for three zero eigenvalues. Counting the allowed k\mathbf kk (Born–von Kármán boundary conditions gives NNN points in the zone, cm-1.6's counting) times 3p3p3p gives 3pN3pN3pN.At each fixed k\mathbf kk, positive atomic masses allow mass weighting of the harmonic equations. The resulting finite 3p3p3p-dimensional dynamical operator is complex Hermitian, hence normal; the complex spectral theorem (ladr 7.31) gives a complete orthonormal eigenbasis with 3p3p3p eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. Hermiticity makes those eigenvalues real, and harmonic stability makes them nonnegative. The three rigid translations are independent zero modes at k=0\mathbf k=0k=0; the stated absence of additional zero modes is needed to call all remaining branches optical. The already counted NNN wave vectors then give 3pN3pN3pN modes.

The mass estimate has no comparable upper-bound guarantee.The inequality step can be made explicit first for a finite-time regularized or discretized path model. text.text: A light-emitting diode is a forward-biased ppp–nnn junction (usually a double heterostructure) in which injected electrons and holes recombine in a thin active layer and the recombination energy leaves as a photon of energy hν≈Egh\nu\approx E_ghν≈Eg​, so the colour is set by the band gap, λ [nm]≈1239.8/Eg [eV]\lambda\,[\text{nm}]\approx1239.8/E_g\,[\text{eV}]λ[nm]≈1239.8/Eg​[eV]. The fraction of injected carriers that give photons is the internal quantum efficiency, in the ABC model ηint=Bn2An+Bn2+Cn3,\eta_{\text{int}}=\frac{Bn^2}{An+Bn^2+Cn^3},ηint​=An+Bn2+Cn3Bn2​, Je d=An+Bn2+Cn3,\frac{J}{e\,d}=An+Bn^2+Cn^3,edJ​=An+Bn2+Cn3, where AAA is the rate of non-radiative (defect) recombination, BBB the radiative coefficient, CCC the Auger coefficient, nnn the carrier density in the active layer of thickness ddd. In a direct-gap material BBB is large; in an indirect-gap material (Si, Ge, GaP) radiative recombination needs a phonon and BBB can be much smaller. The plotted four-order reduction is an assumed comparison, not a universal material ratio.Holds when Spatially uniform ABC model, equal injected electron/hole densities, unit injection efficiency and illustrative positive coefficients A=107A=10^7A=107 s−1^{-1}−1, B=10−10B=10^{-10}B=10−10 (direct) or 10−1410^{-14}10−14 (indirect) cm3^33/s, C=10−30C=10^{-30}C=10−30 cm6^66/s, thickness d=0.1 μd=0.1\,\mud=0.1μm. These are chosen model parameters, not fits or measured silicon data. Presets label photon energies, not calibrated alloy compositions. Internal carrier-to-photon yield is not wall-plug efficiency: extraction, leakage, electrical voltage, heat exchange and spectral width are absent. Cubic loss causes droop in this assumed model; a fit alone does not establish the microscopic cause of droop in a real LED.

Forward bias injects both carrier types into the active layer (cm-4.8); a heterostructure confines them there at densities far above equilibrium, so the product np≫ni2np\gg n_i^2np≫ni2​ and recombination is fast. Each recombination of a conduction-band electron with a valence-band hole releases ≈Eg\approx E_g≈Eg​. Whether this goes into a photon depends on momentum: the selection rule of cm-4.1 makes the radiative rate BnpBnpBnp with a small BBB for indirect gaps, which competes with defect and Auger channels. Efficiency is low at small current (defects: AnA nAn wins), peaks where the defect and Auger losses balance, An=Cn3An=Cn^3An=Cn3, even if Bn2Bn^2Bn2 never dominates, and droops at very high current as the n3n^3n3 Auger term grows.For the positive coefficients used here, the total loss R(n)=An+Bn2+Cn3R(n)=An+Bn^2+Cn^3R(n)=An+Bn2+Cn3 has R′(n)=A+2Bn+3Cn2>0R'(n)=A+2Bn+3Cn^2>0R′(n)=A+2Bn+3Cn2>0 for n≥0n\ge0n≥0. text.text: When electrons are scattered independently by impurities and by lattice vibrations, their scattering rates add and so do the resistivities, ρ(T)=ρimp+ρph(T),\rho(T)=\rho_{\rm imp}+\rho_{\rm ph}(T),ρ(T)=ρimp​+ρph​(T), where the residual resistivity ρimp\rho_{\rm imp}ρimp​ is independent of temperature and proportional to the impurity concentration, and ρph(T)\rho_{\rm ph}(T)ρph​(T) is a property of the pure host. Two samples of the same metal then have parallel ρ(T)\rho(T)ρ(T) curves, with a TTT-independent difference. In the Bloch–Grüneisen form ρph∝T5\rho_{\rm ph}\propto T^5ρph​∝T5 at T≪ΘDT\ll\Theta_DT≪ΘD​ and ∝T\propto T∝T at T≳ΘDT\gtrsim\Theta_DT≳ΘD​.Holds when Independent scattering mechanisms acting on the same carriers on one isotropic Fermi surface. Deviations of a few percent are routine in real metals (anisotropic scattering, multiband conduction, Kondo and size effects), and the rule is only a first approximation at high impurity concentrations.

In the relaxation-time approximation (em-6.4) ρ=m/ne2τ\rho=m/ne^2\tauρ=m/ne2τ and independent collision channels give 1/τ=1/τimp+1/τph(T)1/\tau=1/\tau_{\rm imp}+1/\tau_{\rm ph}(T)1/τ=1/τimp​+1/τph​(T). Impurity scattering is elastic and temperature-independent, phonon scattering freezes out as T→0T\to0T→0 (few phonons, and only small-angle scattering), producing T5T^5T5, while at high TTT the number of phonons is ∝T\propto T∝T. The rule can fail when the scattering rate is not the same for all carriers: with two groups of carriers in parallel the conductivities add and the resistivities do not.Within the stated constant-relaxation-time model, take independent exponential collision waiting times (constant hazards) with positive rates λimp\lambda_{\rm imp}λimp​ and λph\lambda_{\rm ph}λph​. Their no-collision indicators at time t≥0t\ge0t≥0 are bounded independent variables. Factoring the expectation of their product (prob 2.1.13) makes the probability of no collision in either channel the product e−λimpte−λpht=e−(λimp+λph)te^{-\lambda_{\rm imp}t}e^{-\lambda_{\rm ph}t}=e^{-(\lambda_{\rm imp}+\lambda_{\rm ph})t}e−λimp​te−λph​t=e−(λimp​+λph​)t. The mean waiting time is therefore 1/(λimp+λph)1/(\lambda_{\rm imp}+\lambda_{\rm ph})1/(λimp​+λph​). With the same carriers, density and mass in Drude's law, this gives the additive resistivities; it does not justify adding resistivities of separate parallel carrier populations. A zero-rate channel can be omitted; if both rates vanish, this model has no finite collision time.

Switch to two parallel bands (impurities scatter mostly the second band) and the curves are no longer parallel: the difference drifts with TTT, which is the failure of the rule. text.text: A three-dimensional crystal with ppp atoms per primitive cell has exactly 3p3p3p phonon branches ωs(k)\omega_s(\mathbf k)ωs​(k), s=1,…,3ps=1,\dots,3ps=1,…,3p. Assume harmonic stability and no zero-frequency modes at k=0\mathbf k=0k=0 beyond the three rigid translations. Because the crystal is invariant under uniform translation, three of them are acoustic (ω→0\omega\to0ω→0 as k→0\mathbf k\to0k→0) and the remaining 3(p−1)3(p-1)3(p−1) are optical (ω(0)>0\omega(0)>0ω(0)>0). A crystal of NNN cells therefore has 3pN3pN3pN normal modes, one for each degree of freedom, and in the zone each branch has exactly NNN allowed wave vectors.Holds when Harmonic, stable crystals. The value ppp is the number of atoms in the primitive cell; counts of the individual symmetry types of branch (transverse/longitudinal) require the crystal's point group.

For each wave vector the equations of motion form a 3p×3p3p\times3p3p×3p Hermitian dynamical matrix D(k)D(\mathbf k)D(k), so it has 3p3p3p real eigenvalues ω2\omega^2ω2 (nonnegative for a harmonically stable crystal). At k=0\mathbf k=0k=0 a rigid translation of all atoms along xxx, yyy or zzz stretches no bond and so is a zero-frequency eigenvector: this is the acoustic sum rule, equivalent to ∑jΦij=0\sum_{j}\Phi_{ij}=0∑j​Φij​=0 and responsible for three zero eigenvalues. Counting the allowed k\mathbf kk (Born–von Kármán boundary conditions gives NNN points in the zone, cm-1.6's counting) times 3p3p3p gives 3pN3pN3pN.At each fixed k\mathbf kk, positive atomic masses allow mass weighting of the harmonic equations. The resulting finite 3p3p3p-dimensional dynamical operator is complex Hermitian, hence normal; the complex spectral theorem (ladr 7.31) gives a complete orthonormal eigenbasis with 3p3p3p eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. Hermiticity makes those eigenvalues real, and harmonic stability makes them nonnegative. The three rigid translations are independent zero modes at k=0\mathbf k=0k=0; the stated absence of additional zero modes is needed to call all remaining branches optical. The already counted NNN wave vectors then give 3pN3pN3pN modes.

text.text: An electron in an ionic dielectric can move with a cloud of polarization: a polaron. In the continuum Fröhlich model, a parabolic band electron couples to one dispersionless LO phonon branch. Integrating out harmonic phonons leaves a retarded self-interaction of the electron path. Feynman compares this with a quadratic trial action describing an electron attached to an auxiliary particle. A separate small-momentum calculation, Eq. (45), estimates the physical effective mass. It differs from the trial-system total mass (v/w)2(v/w)^2(v/w)2, which is shown separately in the readout. The mass estimate has no comparable upper-bound guarantee.The inequality step can be made explicit first for a finite-time regularized or discretized path model. Normalize the trial measure and let ΔS\Delta SΔS be the real, integrable dimensionless action difference, with finite E0e−ΔS\mathbb E_0 e^{-\Delta S}E0​e−ΔS. Jensen's inequality (rca 3.3) for the convex exponential gives log⁡E0e−ΔS≥−E0ΔS\log\mathbb E_0e^{-\Delta S}\ge-\mathbb E_0\Delta SlogE0​e−ΔS≥−E0​ΔS, so F≤F0+β−1E0ΔSF\le F_0+\beta^{-1}\mathbb E_0\Delta SF≤F0​+β−1E0​ΔS. The physical path-integral and zero-temperature limits supply the ground-state interpretation; the finite-measure inequality alone neither constructs those limits nor certifies a numerical optimizer or the effective-mass estimate.

text.text: A light-emitting diode is a forward-biased ppp–nnn junction (usually a double heterostructure) in which injected electrons and holes recombine in a thin active layer and the recombination energy leaves as a photon of energy hν≈Egh\nu\approx E_ghν≈Eg​, so the colour is set by the band gap, λ [nm]≈1239.8/Eg [eV]\lambda\,[\text{nm}]\approx1239.8/E_g\,[\text{eV}]λ[nm]≈1239.8/Eg​[eV]. The fraction of injected carriers that give photons is the internal quantum efficiency, in the ABC model ηint=Bn2An+Bn2+Cn3,\eta_{\text{int}}=\frac{Bn^2}{An+Bn^2+Cn^3},ηint​=An+Bn2+Cn3Bn2​, Je d=An+Bn2+Cn3,\frac{J}{e\,d}=An+Bn^2+Cn^3,edJ​=An+Bn2+Cn3, where AAA is the rate of non-radiative (defect) recombination, BBB the radiative coefficient, CCC the Auger coefficient, nnn the carrier density in the active layer of thickness ddd. In a direct-gap material BBB is large; in an indirect-gap material (Si, Ge, GaP) radiative recombination needs a phonon and BBB can be much smaller. The plotted four-order reduction is an assumed comparison, not a universal material ratio.Holds when Spatially uniform ABC model, equal injected electron/hole densities, unit injection efficiency and illustrative positive coefficients A=107A=10^7A=107 s−1^{-1}−1, B=10−10B=10^{-10}B=10−10 (direct) or 10−1410^{-14}10−14 (indirect) cm3^33/s, C=10−30C=10^{-30}C=10−30 cm6^66/s, thickness d=0.1 μd=0.1\,\mud=0.1μm. Internal carrier-to-photon yield is not wall-plug efficiency: extraction, leakage, electrical voltage, heat exchange and spectral width are absent. Cubic loss causes droop in this assumed model; a fit alone does not establish the microscopic cause of droop in a real LED.

Forward bias injects both carrier types into the active layer (cm-4.8); a heterostructure confines them there at densities far above equilibrium, so the product np≫ni2np\gg n_i^2np≫ni2​ and recombination is fast. Each recombination of a conduction-band electron with a valence-band hole releases ≈Eg\approx E_g≈Eg​. Whether this goes into a photon depends on momentum: the selection rule of cm-4.1 makes the radiative rate BnpBnpBnp with a small BBB for indirect gaps, which competes with defect and Auger channels. statement-scope.text: When electrons are scattered independently by impurities and by lattice vibrations, their scattering rates add and so do the resistivities, ρ(T)=ρimp+ρph(T),\rho(T)=\rho_{\rm imp}+\rho_{\rm ph}(T),ρ(T)=ρimp​+ρph​(T), where the residual resistivity ρimp\rho_{\rm imp}ρimp​ is independent of temperature and proportional to the impurity concentration, and ρph(T)\rho_{\rm ph}(T)ρph​(T) is a property of the pure host. Two samples of the same metal then have parallel ρ(T)\rho(T)ρ(T) curves, with a TTT-independent difference. In the Bloch–Grüneisen form ρph∝T5\rho_{\rm ph}\propto T^5ρph​∝T5 at T≪ΘDT\ll\Theta_DT≪ΘD​ and ∝T\propto T∝T at T≳ΘDT\gtrsim\Theta_DT≳ΘD​.Independent scattering mechanisms acting on the same carriers on one isotropic Fermi surface. Deviations of a few percent are routine in real metals (anisotropic scattering, multiband conduction, Kondo and size effects), and the rule is only a first approximation at high impurity concentrations.
